lines: The first was a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, born around two and a half thousand years ago in Lumbini, in today's Nepal.
The story goes that his father, a king, wanted him to see nothing sad. No sickness. No old age. No death. Just a perfect palace.
But one day Siddhartha slipped out. And he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body... and a calm wandering monk.
[quietly] One afternoon outside the palace. That's all it took.
At twenty-nine, he left his palace, his wife and his baby son, to find out why people suffer.
After years of searching, he sat under a fig tree at Bodh Gaya and, tradition says, refused to get up until he understood.
When he rose, he was the Buddha: "the awakened one". He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
His answer was a middle way. Not luxury. Not starving yourself. A calm, kind, disciplined life.
Around the same time, another prince, Mahavira, gave up his throne too. He taught ahimsa, non-violence to every living thing, and shaped the religion of Jainism.
[counting on fingers] Two princes. Zero palaces. Very confused royal parents.

lines: The young man was Chandragupta Maurya. His teacher was a sharp, ruthless Brahmin called Chanakya, also known as Kautilya.
The story goes that Chanakya had been insulted at the Nanda court, and swore he would not tie up his hair until the Nandas were destroyed.
[nervous] Rule one of ancient India: never insult the guy with the untied hair.
Around three twenty-one BCE, Chandragupta and Chanakya overthrew the Nandas and took Magadha's capital, Pataliputra, today's Patna.
Then Chandragupta did what nobody had done before. He united most of the subcontinent into one state. The Maurya Empire. Stitch.
When one of Alexander's generals, Seleucus, came to take back the Indian lands, Chandragupta pushed him out and made a deal: land in the northwest for five hundred war elephants.
A Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, lived at Pataliputra and described a huge city of wooden walls, with hundreds of towers and a moat around it.
Chanakya is traditionally credited with the Arthashastra, a handbook on how to run a state: taxes, spies, trade, war. Scholars still debate who exactly wrote it, and when.
[reading] Sir, we have spies watching the merchants...

lines: Tradition says that in old age, Chandragupta gave up his throne, became a Jain monk, and died at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.
His grandson became the most famous ruler in Indian history: Ashoka.
In about two sixty-one BCE, Ashoka invaded Kalinga, in today's Odisha. He won. And the cost horrified him.
We know this because Ashoka told us himself. In an inscription carved in stone, he says a hundred thousand people were killed, and a hundred and fifty thousand were carried away.
Then he wrote something almost no conqueror ever wrote: he was sorry.
[taking off his goggles] An emperor. Apologising. In stone. Read that twice.
Ashoka turned to the teachings of the Buddha. He called his new policy dhamma: kindness, tolerance between religions, care for animals, wells and shade trees along the roads.
He carved his messages on rocks and tall stone pillars across the empire, in a script called Brahmi.
For centuries after, nobody could read it. Until eighteen thirty-seven, when a British scholar, James Prinsep, cracked it, and Ashoka suddenly spoke again.
One of his pillars, at Sarnath, was topped with four lions standing back to back. You know it. It's on every Indian banknote and passport: India's national emblem.
And the wheel beneath the lions, the Ashoka Chakra, sits in the middle of India's flag.
[looking at the flag, impressed] Two thousand years later. Still on the flag.
But empires built by one great man rarely outlive him for long.
About fifty years after Ashoka died, the last Maurya emperor was killed by his own general, during a military parade. The empire broke apart. Shatter.
And into the north, through the mountain passes, came new arrivals once again.

lines: For the next few centuries, India was ruled by many kingdoms at once. And in many ways, it got richer.
The Kushans, who came from Central Asia, built an empire across the north. Their king Kanishka became a great patron of Buddhism. Absorb.
In the south, ships sailed with the monsoon winds to Egypt and Rome, loaded with pepper, cotton cloth and gems.
So much Roman gold flowed to India that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it. He grumbled that India drained Rome of fifty million sesterces every year.
[checking a coin] The Golden Bird. Already collecting gold.
Then, around three hundred twenty CE, a new family united the north again: the Guptas. Stitch.
The Gupta age is often called India's classical age. And the reason is not its battles. It's its ideas.
The poet Kalidasa wrote plays and poems still performed today.
The mathematician Aryabhata, at just twenty-three, wrote that the Earth spins on its own axis... about a thousand years before Copernicus.
He worked out pi to four decimal places: three point one four one six.
And Indian mathematicians were developing the number system you use every day: nine digits, plus a place for nothing.
Just over a century later, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote the rules for zero as a number in its own right. Add, subtract, multiply.
These numerals travelled to the Arab world and then to Europe. Which is why we call them... Arabic numerals.
[confused] So the sky turns around the Earth every night?
No. The Earth turns. The sky stays still.
[looking down at his feet] Then why am I not dizzy?
[patiently] I'll explain tomorrow. If the Earth is still here.

lines: Students came from across Asia to study at Nalanda, one of the world's earliest great universities, with thousands of students and a library so big, it filled several buildings.
Even the iron got better. The Iron Pillar of Delhi, made in the Gupta age, has stood in the open for about sixteen hundred years... and has barely rusted.
[knocking on the pillar] My bicycle rusted in one monsoon.
But in the five hundreds, raiders called the Huna swept in from Central Asia. The Gupta Empire cracked. Shatter. Again.
In the south, though, the story was just getting started.

The Chola kings of Tamil Nadu built one of the greatest navies in Asian history. Rajaraja the First built the vast Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur, finished around ten ten. Its tower is about sixty-six metres tall.
His son, Rajendra, sent his fleet across the Bay of Bengal to attack the mighty Srivijaya kingdom in Sumatra and Malaya.
[looking at a map] An Indian navy. Raiding Southeast Asia. A thousand years ago.
But in the north, things were about to change. A powerful sultan had just learned how rich India's temples were.

lines: His name was Mahmud of Ghazni, from today's Afghanistan. Starting around the year one thousand, he raided north India again and again. Around seventeen times.
He came for gold. His raiders looted cities and temples, including the famous temple of Somnath in Gujarat, in ten twenty-six. Then he went home.
Mahmud didn't stay to rule. But about a hundred and fifty years later, another invader did: Muhammad of Ghor.
In eleven ninety-one, at Tarain, near Delhi, he met the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan. And Prithviraj won. Ghori was wounded and fled.
A year later, Ghori came back with a bigger army. Same battlefield. This time, Prithviraj lost.
[wincing] Rule one of history: if you beat someone, make sure they don't come back next year.
In twelve oh six, Ghori's general Qutb ud-Din Aibak became the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. He began the tallest brick minaret in the world: the Qutb Minar.
Around the same time, according to later chronicles, raiders led by Bakhtiyar Khalji attacked Nalanda, and the great university was ruined.
For the next three hundred years, five different dynasties would rule from Delhi.
One sultan, Alauddin Khalji, beat back several Mongol invasions. Unlike China, Persia and Russia, India was never conquered by the Mongols.
He also tried something very modern: price controls. He fixed the price of grain, horses, cloth, even slaves in the markets of Delhi, and punished cheating shopkeepers harshly.
[taking notes] The first price regulator. Strict. Very, very strict.

lines: Then came the strangest sultan of all: Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Clever, well-read... and full of big ideas.
In thirteen twenty-seven, he decided to move the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, about a thousand kilometres south. And he ordered much of Delhi's population to move with him.
[cheerful] Great news! We are moving the capital. Everybody pack.
[reading the map] It's... forty days' walk.
[whispering] A few years later, he moves everyone back.
He also issued copper and brass coins and declared them worth the same as silver.
Within months, people were making their own coins at home. Huge piles of fake money. He had to buy them all back with real silver.
[shaking his head] Great idea. Five hundred years too early.
In thirteen ninety-eight, the Central Asian conqueror Timur sacked Delhi. The city took a century to recover. Shatter.
Meanwhile, in the south, a powerful Hindu empire was rising: Vijayanagara, with its capital at Hampi. Foreign visitors said it was as big as Rome, and full of diamonds and horses.
But here's the thing about the Sultanate years. Something new was also being made.

Persian and Indian builders mixed their styles in arches, domes and minarets. The poet Amir Khusrau wrote in a mix of Persian and the local speech, and is traditionally credited with shaping qawwali music.
Out of the bazaars and army camps, a whole new language grew: what would become Urdu, and close cousin to Hindi.
[smiling] India doesn't just get invaded. It gets... remixed.
In fifteen twenty-six, a young prince from Central Asia rode down from Kabul. He had lost his homeland more than once. He was looking for a new one.
His great-great-great-grandfather was Timur. And on his mother's side, he was descended from Genghis Khan.

lines: His name was Babur. And at Panipat, north of Delhi, he faced the Sultan Ibrahim Lodi, who had a far bigger army and around a hundred elephants.
But Babur brought something new to India: cannons and guns. The elephants panicked. In a single day, the Sultanate was gone.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire. Stitch, again.
He also wrote a remarkable memoir, the Baburnama. And honestly? He wasn't that impressed with India.
He complained there were no good horses, no good grapes, and no good melons.
[proudly] Your Majesty, the finest mangoes in Hindustan!
[writing gloomily] Day four hundred. Still no melons.
Babur ruled for only four years. His son Humayun lost the whole empire to an Afghan general, Sher Shah Suri.
Sher Shah ruled for just five years, but he was brilliant. He improved the great road from Bengal to the northwest, later called the Grand Trunk Road, with rest houses and wells along the way.
And he issued a new silver coin. He called it the rupiya.
[holding up a coin] The rupee. Started by the guy who kicked the Mughals out.

lines: Humayun came back fifteen years later and took Delhi again. A few months later, he slipped on the stairs of his library and died.
His son was thirteen years old. His name was Akbar.
In fifteen fifty-six, at a second battle at Panipat, Akbar's army defeated the general Hemu. And over the next fifty years, Akbar built one of the richest empires on Earth.
Akbar's secret weapon was not cannons. It was including people.
He made alliances with the Rajput kingdoms, many through marriage, and gave Rajput princes high posts in his army.
He scrapped the jizya, a tax paid by non-Muslims. And his finance minister, Raja Todar Mal, built a careful system for measuring land and setting taxes.
Akbar could barely read. Yet he collected a huge library, and had books read aloud to him every day.
At his new city, Fatehpur Sikri, he built a hall where Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars debated religion in front of him.
[whispering] The debates got so heated, the Emperor had to play referee.

Not everyone accepted Akbar. The Rajput ruler of Mewar, Maharana Pratap, refused to submit, and fought Akbar's army at Haldighati in fifteen seventy-six. He kept resisting from the hills for the rest of his life.
Still, by the time Akbar died in sixteen oh five, the Mughal Empire was enormous. And it was only getting richer.
Remember the hook? That quarter of the world's economy? That was the India his grandson would rule.
[checking his watch, excited] Now we're getting to the gold.

lines: Akbar's son Jahangir loved art, gardens and wine, and his court painters made some of the most beautiful miniatures ever painted.
The real power behind his throne was often his wife, Nur Jahan. She issued orders, minted coins in her own name... and once, the story goes, shot a tiger from the back of an elephant.
[impressed] Coins with her name on them. That's real power.
Then came Shah Jahan. And under him, the Mughal Empire reached its peak of wealth and show.
He sat on the Peacock Throne, covered in gold and jewels. It reportedly took seven years to make.
And when his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their fourteenth child, he built her a tomb on the river at Agra.
Around twenty thousand workers and craftsmen, more than twenty years. White marble from Rajasthan, inlaid with stones from across Asia.
In this age, India was one of the richest places on Earth. Indian cotton cloth dressed half the world. Silver poured in from Europe to pay for it.
This was the Golden Bird at its brightest. Shine.
[pointing at the Taj] Remember the quarter of the world's economy? You're looking at it.
But Shah Jahan's sons fought a brutal war for the throne. The winner was Aurangzeb.
He had his brothers killed... and locked his own father inside Agra Fort, where, the story goes, Shah Jahan spent his last years gazing across the river at the Taj.
[not turning] Is my son coming to visit?
[sighing] Regards. I gave him an empire.
